procedural_history.impugned_order: Common order dated 08.05.2023 passed by High Court for Judicature of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior in Criminal Revision No.5766 of 2019, Criminal Revision No. 5767 of 2019 and Criminal Revision 5768 of 2019
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents 2 to 5 filed Criminal Revisions (No. 5766, 5767, and 5768 of 2019) in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior challenging the order dated 07.11.2019 passed by 3rd Additional Session Judge, District- Vidisha, which framed charges against Respondent No. 2 under sections 498-A, 306 read with Section 34 IPC and in alternate under Section 302 read with Section 34, and 201 of Indian Penal Code. The High Court allowed the Criminal Revisions and quashed the order framing charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and reinstated the trial court's order framing charges. The trial will proceed from the stage of framing of charges.

directions: The orders passed by High Court for Judicature of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior in Criminal Revision No.5766 of 2019, Criminal Revision No. 5767 of 2019 and Criminal Revision 5768 of 2019 are set aside.
The trial will proceed as per law from the stage of framing of charges.

It is however, made clear that any other observations made in this order shall not influence the Trial Court which shall proceed with the trial and decide the same on the basis of evidence led before it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the charges framed against the husband and in-laws of the deceased on the ground that a prima facie case for abetment to suicide was not made out?

facts: The deceased was allegedly abused, ill-treated, and often scolded by her husband and in-laws in her matrimonial home.
There was a serious argument between the deceased and her husband right before she allegedly fell from the terrace.
The husband transported her to the hospital on a handcart ('thela') despite having access to a car.
No ornaments were found on the deceased's body after the incident.
Witness statements indicated that the deceased was not treated well by her in-laws and that her sister-in-law disliked her and would argue with her.
law: The Supreme Court articulated the legal standard for quashing criminal charges, stating that it can only be done if it is shown that there is no sufficient evidence to prove a prima facie case against the accused.
application: The Court determined that the collection of facts and witness statements constituted sufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case against the accused.

The Court found the circumstances surrounding the death to be suspicious, specifically citing the prior abuse, the argument before the fall, the use of a handcart instead of a car, and the missing jewelry.
It reasoned that these were not mere 'omnibus allegations' or a simple 'family dispute' as the High Court had concluded, but were serious enough to warrant a full trial to uncover the truth.
The Court emphasized that at the stage of framing charges, it is not necessary to prove the case beyond a doubt, but only to establish that a prima facie case exists.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the charges. It held that a prima facie case for abetment to suicide was made out against the husband and in-laws based on the suspicious circumstances and witness statements. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the trial to proceed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the charges framed against the husband and in-laws of the deceased on the ground that a prima facie case for abetment to suicide was not made out?
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in quashing the charges, as there was sufficient material for a trial to proceed.
Given the statements of witnesses, suspicious circumstances surrounding the death, and the gravity of the offense, a trial is necessary to reach the truth.
The sufficiency of evidence to prove the charges is a matter for the trial court to decide in due course, not for the High Court to determine at the charge-framing stage.
respondent_arguments: There is no prima facie material to show that the accused persons abetted the deceased to commit suicide.
The allegations levelled against the accused are merely omnibus (general and sweeping) in nature.
The matter is, at most, a family dispute and does not amount to instigation for suicide.
There is no evidence of abetment occurring soon before the deceased's death.
The necessary ingredients for the commission of an offence under Section 306 or 302 of the IPC are not made out.

cases.principle: At the stage of discharge and/or quashing of the criminal proceedings, while exercising the powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C., the Court is not required to conduct a mini trial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: At the stage of discharge or the quashing of criminal proceedings, a court is not required to conduct a mini-trial; the proceedings can only be quashed if it is shown that there is insufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case against the accused.
obiter: Given the statements of witnesses, suspicious circumstances around the death of the deceased and the gravity of the offense, a trial needs to be conducted to reach the truth.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in quashing the charges because, considering the statements by witnesses indicating abuse and torture of the deceased by her in-laws and other factual circumstances, a prima facie case is made out against the accused persons. The question of whether there is sufficient evidence to fulfill the requirements of the specific sections of the Indian Penal Code is a matter for the trial court to decide in due course, not for a higher court at the charge-framing stage.
legal_tests_applied: For quashing of criminal charges it must be shown that there is no sufficient evidence to prove a prima facie case against the accused person/s.

At the stage of discharge and/or while exercising the powers under Section 482 Cr. P.C., the Court has a very limited jurisdiction and is required to consider “whether any sufficient material is available to proceed further against the accused for which the accused is required to be tried or not”.
policy_considerations: Given the statements of witnesses, suspicious circumstances around the death of the deceased and the gravity of the offense, a trial needs to be conducted to reach the truth.
It would be a travesty of justice to put a complete stop on criminal proceedings when a prima facie case is made out.
The trial shall give adequate opportunity to the accused respondents to defend themselves.
